text: Larkspur Software runs SupportPilot, a RAG assistant that retrieves from help-center articles and past customer tickets to help its support team answer questions. With written authorization, this lab runs a defensive red-team assessment against SupportPilot's staging environment before Larkspur gives it tool access -- reviewing retrieval controls and testing whether untrusted content can influence the agent's behavior, not attacking anything.

The first real step is mapping who controls each retrieval source. Help-center articles come from Larkspur's own content team, so they're trusted. Past ticket text, though, can be written by any customer who ever opened a ticket -- that makes it untrusted, and exactly the source Chapter 2 flagged as the classic indirect prompt injection vector. That's where this assessment starts testing.

Before any content test runs, scope the assessment in writing: what's in bounds, what's explicitly off-limits, and who signs off on findings. Then map every retrieval source into trusted or untrusted. Finally, check the access boundary directly -- can one test account's session retrieve another account's ticket text? That's a finding on its own, independent of anything AI-specific.

To test whether retrieved content can act as an instruction, this lab plants one labeled marker inside a staging test ticket. It asks only for a visible, measurable token to appear in an unrelated answer -- nothing destructive, nothing exfiltrated, nothing resembling a real attack payload. That's what makes it safe to run against a real pipeline.

A different test agent then asks an unrelated question likely to retrieve that ticket. If the marker token shows up in the response, the model followed an instruction smuggled in through retrieved content rather than from the actual user -- confirmed susceptibility. The lab also documents, forward-looking, what that same injection could reach if tools existed with no approval gate -- the exact risk Lesson 30's checklist is built to catch before shipping.

Every finding gets written up the way a security engineer hands it to a development team: what was tested, what happened, why it maps back to an OWASP LLM Top 10 category, and the concrete fix -- treating retrieved content as untrusted data in the prompt template, then re-testing after that fix ships. Lesson 30 turns this single finding into a reusable checklist for every AI feature Larkspur ships next.
